title: The son on the mountain
hookLine: Nuh's own son refuses the ark, says a mountain will save him, and the waves come between them (11:42–43)

lines: ONE FACE, AS THE WATER RISES.
cards: Waves like mountains, the Qur'an says. A ship rides them, carrying the few who believed. And from the deck, a father sees his son, standing apart, as the water rises.
Many families have someone like that son. The one you can't reach. The brother who stopped answering.
The daughter who moved across the country and calls twice a year. You love them, you've tried everything, and they're still on the other side of something you can't cross.

teach.h: O MY SON! COME RIDE WITH US.
teach.b: Surah eleven. Nuh calls to his son, in Pickthall's words: “O my son! Come ride with us.” After nine hundred and fifty years of calling his own people, the last call in the story is a father calling his child.

The son answers, paraphrasing: I'll go up a mountain; it will keep me safe from the water. He trusts the highest thing he can see. Nuh answers: today nothing can protect from God's command, except the one He has mercy on.

teach.h: THE WAVE CAME IN BETWEEN THEM.
teach.b: Then one of the saddest lines in the Qur'an: “And the wave came in between them.” No speech. A wave, between a father and a son.
The Qur'an doesn't name the son; tradition calls him Kan'an. But it doesn't end there. When the water settles and the ship rests on a mountain called al-Judi, Nuh turns to God.
Paraphrasing: my Lord, my son was of my family, and Your promise is true.
He's still calling. God answers gently but firmly: he is not of your family, his conduct was not right; don't ask Me about what you don't know. And Nuh asks forgiveness for even asking.
Many commentators say family, in this answer, means the family of faith, not blood.
What everyone notices is the father: a prophet who could accept anything from God, still reaching for his son, right to the end.

how: Muslims read Nuh's call to his son in surah eleven, and many parents recall it when a child has turned away: faith can't be handed down, but a parent keeps praying.

practice: Bring to mind someone you can't reach right now: far away, estranged, or just closed off. Don't rehearse the argument; just hold their face for a few breaths.
If you pray, pray for them in your own words, the way Nuh kept asking for his son; if you don't, wish them well, silently, as if across water.

wordCard.voice: Kan'an, the name tradition gives Nuh's son, who trusted a mountain over the ship, and was lost in the wave.

orig.note: Arabic: "O my little son," a tender form Nuh uses in 11:42; Luqman uses it too.
